posts.content_md:
While flying home from Brazil, I had time to do some thought experiments. I just came in my house and I cannot wait to ask some more questions. And collect enough knowledge for making my own plates. Here goes:

1] When immersing the plate in the LiBr+dye bath (after having loaded with AgNo3), what determines the fial size of the created AgBr+dye crystals? Is it the time during which the plate is soaked in the LiBr? Does the dye have something to do with it?

2] If the time factor is the most important, why is it then that when you make panchromatic plates and do the second soak in LiBr+second dye that the new deposits of AgBr don't attach to the already existing crystals? Or do they attach to them and make them bigger, thus degrading the resolution of the film? Or does the previous dye prevent the newly dyed deposits from attaching to it's own crystals?

3] Would it in that case be possible to make higher concentrations of small crystals by using different dyes for the same wavelength and doing several soaks with these different dyes?

4] Would it be advantagious to have crystals of different sizes in one emulsion or is it better to have them all of the same size? I can imagine if they would all be of the same size it would be more difficult to record gradients of intensities, i.e. the exposed+developed film would become more newspaper like black/white dithering.

5] If it is an advantage to have crystals of different sizes, might it be a good idea to repeat the AgNO3 -> LiBr+dye steps a few times with shorter baths in the LiBr and thus with each step increasing the size of the already existing crystals a little, but also introducing fresh super small crystals? I imagine that having more crystals would help in sensitivity and resolution, and having the different sizes would help with gradients and thus increase the bandwidth of the film.

6] If it is just the amount of similar sized crystals that's important, would it be possible to do several soaks with some kind of magical growth blocker saok in-between the baths that encapsulates the already existing crystals in a similar way that pyrogallol can encapsulate already exposed crystals?

I'm sorry to take up your time with my silly questions. I promise I will order the Bjelkhagen book tomorrow. Perhaps I can answer some questions of other people after I have read it.

posts.author: jeff-blyth
posts.content_md:
> **Hans:** While flying home from Brazil, I had time to do some thought experiments. I just came in my house and I cannot wait to ask some more questions. And collect enough knowledge for making my own plates. Here goes:1] When immersing the plate in the LiBr+dye bath (after having loaded with AgNo3), what determines the final size of the created AgBr+dye crystals? Is it the time during which the plate is soaked in the LiBr? Does the dye have something to do with it?Yes you are right apparently (I can only say from what I have observed)If you dont soak the plate long enough to make all the dissolved AgNO3 in the gelatin layer be converted to AgBr then you get the smallest grains but the bit of unconverted AgNO3 causes trouble by instantly turning into black silver the moment it touches any reducing agent such as the recommended ascorbate sensitizer bath let alone the developer. So this means chemical fogging which by definition means developed silver independent of any light. If on the other hand you leave the plate in the LiBr for too long eg for say 10 minutes, you do get bigger grains and scatter. Fortunately the recommended dyes in my article are both powerful grain growth restrainers as well as the gelatin itself. So the system is very forgiving and 2 minutes to 3 minutes can be OK . Your previous post brought up the matter of film thickness and you can see here that with thick layers you have got to give longer times and these times are not linearly related to thickness and it can involve those awful equations of Fick's "law of diffusion". [In certain other polymers I occasionally use to make "Smart Holograms" that act as sensors I do have trouble with them promoting grain growth so I have to keep the time in the LiBr bath down to about 30 sec. and then vigorously rinse to get the LiBr out , I then give a lot more rinsing to get any unconverted AgNO3 out].2] If the time factor is the most important, why is it then that when you make panchromatic plates and do the second soak in LiBr+second dye that the new deposits of AgBr don't attach to the already existing crystals? Or do they attach to them and make them bigger, thus degrading the resolution of the film? Or does the previous dye prevent the newly dyed deposits from attaching to it's own crystals?I can only guess that your last question is also the right answer. But I am not sure.3] Would it in that case be possible to make higher concentrations of small crystals by using different dyes for the same wavelength and doing several soaks with these different dyes?I do not follow your reasoning here.4] Would it be advantagious to have crystals of different sizes in one emulsion or is it better to have them all of the same size? I can imagine if they would all be of the same size it would be more difficult to record gradients of intensities, i.e. the exposed+developed film would become more newspaper like black/white dithering.See Martin's comment. I think of this diffraction business as a natural digital phenomenon.-----It either causes diffraction or it does'nt---- there is no gray scale involved other than that created by noise and scatter.5] If it is an advantage to have crystals of different sizes, might it be a good idea to repeat the AgNO3 -> LiBr+dye steps a few times with shorter baths in the LiBr and thus with each step increasing the size of the already existing crystals a little, but also introducing fresh super small crystals? I imagine that having more crystals would help in sensitivity and resolution, and having the different sizes would help with gradients and thus increase the bandwidth of the film.See my comments on your comments!6] If it is just the amount of similar sized crystals that's important, would it be possible to do several soaks with some kind of magical growth blocker saok in-between the baths that encapsulates the already existing crystals in a similar way that pyrogallol can encapsulate already exposed crystals?I always consider the ideal size is to work towards zero size! Obviously there must be a physical size ultimately but I never have to worry about that end of it !I'm sorry to take up your time with my silly questions. I promise I will order the Bjelkhagen book tomorrow. Perhaps I can answer some questions of other people after I have read it.

Hans I have to say sincerely that from the point of view of making a good living you should continue to fly planes, but from the point of view of advancing Science and making new technological contributions you should be in a research lab.... where your questioning mind would be a huge asset !

Jeff

posts.author: Hans
posts.content_md:
Hi, thank you for your always clear and understandable answers. 

The idea behind question 3 was that if a dyed crystal prohibits growing of differently dyed AgBr depositing on it, it might be possible to increase the amount of crystals by doing several baths with different dye-types (for the same wavelength) on the same plate without increasing the size of the already deposited crystals.

I thought that having the ability to record intensity gradients might make it possible to create more sinewave like patterns on the plate. Also, I have some nagging intuitive feeling that it might help in the recording of the intensity of a certain diffracted interference pattern.

For example, if I want to record the following pattern:

"*-------**-----***---******---***-----**-------*"

A simple digital double slit (ie three vertical rows of digital grains) would do in this case. But if I also would want to have this pattern a certain brightness, it would help to have these grains of a certain size that corresponds to the correct amount of reflection/transmittance. Otherwise I would need a more complex digitally dithered pattern and thus eat up a lot more bandwidth of the available surface on the film. Or perhaps I am thinking in a wrong direction here. Also I have a feeling that differently gradiated grains (pixels) could do more than one function at the same time (be part of more than one diffraction pattern at the same time) and help create more perfect interference patterns for creating more complex intermingled diffractions. 

I should learn how to calculate Fourier maths I suppose. Does anyone know of a Fourier tutorial that explains this theory to high school graduates? (I remember all my old maths, including the second order linear differential equations and complex numbers)

Jeff, you are right. I chose flying because of the security and the sense of adventure. But at times I do feel a great sadness that I did not decide to become a scientist. My dream would be be involved in a small business that involves something with holography, in which I could do lots of research and become a part-time aviator. But I guess it's easy to think up lots of questions in my position because I lack so much knowledge to put brakes on potentially silly idea's.

(I remember all my old maths, including the second order linear differential equations and complex numbers)If a dye A gets more energy than a dye B when combining with an AgBr ion-pair ( molecule) then when both dyes are in solution together there will be a trend for dye A to occupy the binding sites on virgin AgBr ion pairs rather than dye B. But if dye B is already combined with AgBr from a previous step then it takes more energy for A to displace B than to go for a virgin AgBr. So with the limited time the liquid phase is available dye B can survive on the grain. I do not know the ratio of dye molecules to AgBrgrainsI would like to know the rough answer to this. (obviously individual AgBr ionpairs vastly outnumber the dye molecules.)With the large numbers of individual ionpairs in even the smallest AgBr grains obviously both dyes can be attached to each grain so either can cause light induced damage to the grain . If a grain is in the node zone of one wavelength but in the antinode zone of the other wavelength then thatmeans that one dye alone is active and I intuitively feel that this is better than the case where both wavelengths affect the grain because it is in the antinode of both although that's inevitably happening. So the doubly activated grains get more exposure .It may mean that you need panchromatic emulsions to be even finer thanmonochromatic ones to offset this .We dont want a gradient of sizes,---- it has been a problem for manufacturers of fine grained emulsion coatings to have a really fine grained coating ruined by a tiny proportion of large grains known as "rocks". The scatter from these is very high inspite of their very low proportion . This follows from the Rayleigh scatter theory that scatter is proportional to the sixth power of the diameter of the particle , assuming it is spherical. posts.author: Hans
posts.content_md:
Thank you, I think I understand now why a dye has a preference to combine with virgin AgBr, and why it's better to do separate soaks for panchromatic emulsions rather than just soaking in a cocktail of multiple dyes+LiBr.

I also meant binary when I wrote "digital".

I never thought of the possibility of scattering light from larger grains. In that case it does indeed make a lot of sense to make the grains as small as possible. I guess ideal would be smaller than the wavelength of the light used, so the light could bend around the grain, just like sound can travel around a coke bottle but has difficulty of bending around a truck. But perhaps a particle smaller than the wavelength would have trouble absorbing the energy of the photons. If that is the case I guess there should be an ideal size for the particles. 

I just ordered the Bjelkhagen book. (Can't wait to start reading it)

I have a flight again tonight, I am sure many little idea's will emerge on my way over the big pond. I should be back just before Christmas with more questions.

Thank you again.
